claims.text: Formation of a protective oxide layer through surface engineering can improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Combined Cr and Al alloying additions promote formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer.
The proposed intervention should operate in an oxidizing atmosphere at 1000-1200°C for exposures up to 100 hours.
The oxide layer formed by the intervention will be stable and adherent under the stated conditions.
A stable and adherent oxide layer prevents oxygen penetration into the alloy.
Preventing oxygen penetration reduces the alloy's oxidation rate.
The Cr- and Al-alloyed material will exhibit a 20-50% improvement in high-temperature oxygen resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
A comparison of weight gain, oxide-layer thickness, and microstructure between alloyed and untreated materials can test the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies surface engineering as the intervention, whereas the intervention field specifies Cr and Al alloying additions, which ordinarily change bulk composition unless explicitly described as surface alloying.

The comparison is described as alloyed versus untreated material. Alloying changes composition rather than merely treating the same alloy, so 'untreated alloy' does not clearly define a composition-matched baseline.
